khat.name: Khat
khat.summary: A flowering shrub native to eastern and southern Africa whose leaves are chewed as a mild stimulant causing sociability and euphoria; long cultivated in Ethiopia and widely consumed in Somalia and Yemen.

richard-francis-burton.name: Richard Francis Burton
richard-francis-burton.summary: British explorer, scholar and army officer (1821–1890) who spoke up to 29 languages, searched for the source of the Nile, made a disguised pilgrimage to Mecca, translated One Thousand and One Nights, and published the Kama Sutra in English.

emirate-of-harar.name: Emirate of Harar
emirate-of-harar.summary: A Muslim kingdom founded in 1647 in what is now eastern Ethiopia, controlling major trade routes before its influence declined in the 19th century and it was eventually annexed by the Ethiopian Empire.

harar.name: Harar
harar.summary: Walled city in eastern Ethiopia, a long-standing trading hub linking the Horn of Africa to Arabia and beyond, called by UNESCO the 'fourth holiest city' of Islam.

peaberry.name: Peaberry
peaberry.summary: A type of coffee bean that forms as a single rounded seed instead of the usual two flat-sided beans, making up about 5% of harvested beans and prized for complex flavor.

berbera.name: Berbera
berbera.summary: A coastal port city in Somaliland, once a major trading hub on the Somali seaboard and later capital of British Somaliland from 1884 to 1941.

mokha.name: Mokha
mokha.summary: A Red Sea port city in Yemen that was the principal port for Yemen's capital and, from the 16th to 19th centuries, the world's main marketplace for coffee, giving its name to 'mocha'.

st-george-s-cathedral-addis-ababa.name: St. George's Cathedral, Addis Ababa
st-george-s-cathedral-addis-ababa.summary: An Ethiopian Orthodox cathedral in Addis Ababa known for its distinctive octagonal form.

sebastiano-castagna.name: Sebastiano Castagna
sebastiano-castagna.summary: An Italian engineer (1868-1938) awarded the Gold Medal of Military Valour for his service in Italian East Africa.

zewditu.name: Zewditu
zewditu.summary: Empress of Ethiopia from 1916 to 1930, the empire's only reigning empress, crowned in 1917 and known for conservative policies resisting the modernizing reforms of her regent, later Emperor Haile Selassie I.

fasil-ghebbi.name: Fasil Ghebbi
fasil-ghebbi.summary: A 17th-century fortress complex in Gondar, Ethiopia, founded by Emperor Fasilides, showing Portuguese, Hindu, and Arab architectural influences and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gondar.name: Gondar
gondar.summary: City in Ethiopia's Amhara Region, former capital of the Ethiopian Empire and Begemder Province, known for its royal castles at the Fasil Ghebbi UNESCO site.

dervish-movement-somali.name: Dervish State
dervish-movement-somali.summary: An armed resistance movement and polity based at Taleh in Somalia from 1895 to 1920, led by Sayyid Mohamed against British and Italian colonial rule, drawing fighters from many clans.

taleh.name: Taleh
taleh.summary: A historical town in Somalia that served as the capital of the pre-independence Dervish state, home to a large fortress complex.

british-expedition-to-abyssinia.name: British Expedition to Abyssinia
british-expedition-to-abyssinia.summary: An 1868 British rescue and punitive mission against Emperor Tewodros II of Ethiopia, led by General Robert Napier, which freed British hostages and captured the Ethiopian capital.

tewodros-ii.name: Tewodros II
tewodros-ii.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1855 to 1868 whose rule is seen as the start of modern Ethiopia, ending the fractured Era of the Princes, though he never fully restored a strong monarchy.

william-wright-orientalist.name: William Wright
william-wright-orientalist.summary: English Orientalist and Cambridge professor of Arabic (1830–1889), known for cataloguing manuscript collections and his widely used Arabic grammar book.

church-mission-society.name: Church Mission Society
church-mission-society.summary: A British Anglican mission organization founded in 1799 that worked internationally and gave rise to independent daughter societies around the world.

karl-wilhelm-isenberg.name: Karl Wilhelm Isenberg
karl-wilhelm-isenberg.summary: German missionary and linguist (1806-1864) who compiled a dictionary and grammar of Amharic and translated religious texts into Marathi and Amharic.

johann-ludwig-krapf.name: Johann Ludwig Krapf
johann-ludwig-krapf.summary: German missionary and explorer (1810–1881) who, with Johannes Rebmann, was among the first Europeans to see Mount Kenya and Kilimanjaro, and translated the New Testament into the Kamba language.

dhaanto.name: Dhaanto
dhaanto.summary: A traditional Somali style of music and folk dance native to the Somali people of the Horn of Africa.

august-dillmann.name: August Dillmann
august-dillmann.summary: German orientalist and biblical scholar who lived from 1823 to 1894.

george-annesley-2nd-earl-of-mountnorris.name: George Annesley, 2nd Earl of Mountnorris
george-annesley-2nd-earl-of-mountnorris.summary: British peer and politician (1770–1844), styled Viscount Valentia between 1793 and 1816 before becoming the 2nd Earl of Mountnorris.

john-rylands-research-institute-and-libr.name: John Rylands Library
john-rylands-research-institute-and-libr.summary: Neo-Gothic library in Manchester, opened 1900, founded by Enriqueta Rylands in memory of her husband and now part of the University of Manchester's special collections.
john-rylands-research-institute-and-libr.source_title: John Rylands Research Institute and Library

fetha-negest.name: Fetha Negest
fetha-negest.summary: A theocratic legal code compiled around 1240 by a Coptic Egyptian writer, later translated into Ge'ez in Ethiopia and used as its supreme law until 1931.

menelik-ii.name: Menelik II
menelik-ii.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913, who expanded the empire to its greatest historical extent and defeated Italian colonial forces at the Battle of Adwa in 1896.

oreste-baratieri.name: Oreste Baratieri
oreste-baratieri.summary: Italian military officer (1841–1901) who served as governor of Eritrea from 1892 to 1896 and commanded Italian colonial forces.

adwa.name: Adwa
adwa.summary: Town in Ethiopia's Tigray Region, best known as the site near the 1896 Battle of Adwa, where Ethiopian forces defeated Italian troops.

first-italo-ethiopian-war.name: First Italo-Ethiopian War
first-italo-ethiopian-war.summary: War fought between Italy and Ethiopia in 1895–1896, ending in Ethiopian victory at the Battle of Adwa, one of the first decisive African victories over a European colonial power.

second-italo-ethiopian-war.name: Second Italo-Ethiopian War
second-italo-ethiopian-war.summary: Italy's invasion of Ethiopia from 1935 to 1936, regarded as the largest colonial campaign in history, in which Mussolini authorized the use of mustard gas against Ethiopian forces.

egyptian-ethiopian-war.name: Egyptian–Ethiopian War
egyptian-ethiopian-war.summary: An 1874–1876 war in which Ethiopia defeated the Khedivate of Egypt, securing its independence just before the Scramble for Africa and blunting Egypt's regional ambitions.

scramble-for-africa.name: Scramble for Africa
scramble-for-africa.summary: The invasion, conquest and colonisation of most of Africa by seven Western European powers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, regulated by the 1884-85 Berlin Conference.

battle-of-magdala.name: Battle of Magdala
battle-of-magdala.summary: 1868 battle that concluded the British Expedition to Abyssinia, in which British forces under Robert Napier defeated Emperor Tewodros II at Magdala, 390 miles from the Red Sea.

robert-napier-1st-baron-napier-of-magdal.name: Robert Napier
robert-napier-1st-baron-napier-of-magdal.summary: British Indian Army officer (1810–1890) who led the British Expedition to Abyssinia in 1867, defeating Emperor Tewodros II with minimal losses and rescuing British hostages.
robert-napier-1st-baron-napier-of-magdal.source_title: Robert Napier, 1st Baron Napier of Magdala

treaty-of-wuchale.name: Treaty of Wuchale
treaty-of-wuchale.summary: 1889 treaty between Ethiopia and Italy meant to secure friendship and trade, but differing Italian and Amharic wording on a protectorate clause led to the First Italo-Ethiopian War.

gura-eritrea.name: Gura, Eritrea
gura-eritrea.summary: A settlement in Eritrea's Debub region, in the Gura Valley of the southeastern Eritrean Highlands, about 32 kilometres southeast of the capital Asmara.

ras-alula.name: Ras Alula
ras-alula.summary: Ethiopian general and politician (c. 1847–1897) who led Abyssinian forces against Ottoman Egypt, the Mahdists and Italy, called Ethiopia's greatest leader since Tewodros II.

jubba-river.name: Jubba River
jubba-river.summary: A river in southern Somalia flowing from the Ethiopian border south to the Somali Sea, giving its name to the surrounding Jubaland region.

yusuf-mahamud-ibrahim.name: Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim
yusuf-mahamud-ibrahim.summary: Third and most powerful Sultan of the Somali Geledi sultanate (r. 1798–1848), under whom the kingdom reached its wealthiest peak in East Africa.

sultanate-of-the-geledi.name: Geledi Sultanate
sultanate-of-the-geledi.summary: A Somali kingdom, also called the Gobroon dynasty, that ruled parts of the Horn of Africa from the late 1600s to the early 1900s, peaking under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim before its absorption into Italian Somaliland in 1911.

battle-of-adwa.name: Battle of Adwa
battle-of-adwa.summary: The climactic 1 March 1896 battle of the First Italo-Ethiopian War, in which Emperor Menelik II's Ethiopian army defeated an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri, securing Ethiopian independence.

tigray-region.name: Tigray Region
tigray-region.summary: The northernmost regional state of Ethiopia, homeland of the Tigrayan, Irob and Kunama peoples, with Mekelle as its capital.

thaddeus-p-mott.name: Thaddeus P. Mott
thaddeus-p-mott.summary: American soldier of fortune and former Union Army officer who fought in several countries' wars and recruited American veterans to modernize the Egyptian army in the 1870s.

william-wing-loring.name: William Wing Loring
william-wing-loring.summary: An American soldier, politician, and lawyer who served in the U.S., Confederate, and Egyptian armies; a Mexican-American War veteran and one of the Army's youngest colonels, he was later made a Fereek Pasha in Egypt (1818–1886).

yohannes-iv.name: Yohannes IV
yohannes-iv.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia from 1871 to 1889, previously king of Tigray from 1869; he defeated a large-scale Egyptian invasion and worked to strengthen Christian dominance in Ethiopia.

tekle-giyorgis-ii.name: Tekle Giyorgis II
tekle-giyorgis-ii.summary: Emperor of Ethiopia, born Wagshum Gobeze, who ruled from 1868 to 1871 before being wounded and captured in battle and later dying in captivity.

john-kirkham-adventurer.name: John Kirkham
john-kirkham-adventurer.summary: British adventurer who became chief Western military advisor to Ethiopian Emperor Yohannes IV, training troops, fighting successfully at Adwa in 1871, and later serving as a provincial governor; he died in 1876.

massawa.name: Massawa
massawa.summary: A Red Sea port city in Eritrea, ruled over the centuries by the Dahlak Sultanate, the Ottomans, Egypt, and Italy; it was capital of Italian Eritrea until 1897.

gallabat.name: Gallabat
gallabat.summary: A village in Sudan's Al Qadarif state on the border with Ethiopia, opposite the Ethiopian village of Metemma.

dembiya.name: Dembiya
dembiya.summary: A historic region of Ethiopia near Lake Tana, bordered by Wogera, Begemder, Gojjam and Agaw lands, later folded into Begemder province.

ge-ez.name: Ge'ez
ge-ez.summary: Ancient South Semitic language from Ethiopia and Eritrea, still used today as the liturgical language of Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox and Catholic churches.

amharic.name: Amharic
amharic.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language and Ethiopia's official working language, spoken by over 58 million people; it is the second most widely spoken Semitic language after Arabic.

tigrinya-language.name: Tigrinya language
tigrinya-language.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language spoken by Tigrinya and Tigrayan peoples in Eritrea and Ethiopia, which developed separately from Ge'ez.

tigre-language.name: Tigre language
tigre-language.summary: An Ethio-Semitic language spoken mainly by the Tigre people of western Eritrea, closely related to Ge'ez, with about 800,000 speakers as of 1997.

amhara-region.name: Amhara Region
amhara-region.summary: A regional state in northern Ethiopia, homeland of the Amhara and other peoples, containing Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile, and Ethiopia's highest peak.

shewa.name: Shewa
shewa.summary: A historical region of Ethiopia, once an autonomous kingdom within the Ethiopian Empire, whose territory includes the modern capital Addis Ababa.

ishaaq-bin-ahmed.name: Sheikh Ishaaq
ishaaq-bin-ahmed.summary: Semi-legendary Islamic scholar said to have traveled from Arabia to the Horn of Africa in the 10th or 11th century and settled at Maydh, traditionally regarded as forefather of the Somali Isaaq clan-family.

maydh.name: Maydh
maydh.summary: An ancient port city in Somaliland's eastern Sanaag region, where the semi-legendary 10th-century Sheikh Ishaaq is said to have settled after crossing from Arabia.

begemder.name: Begemder
begemder.summary: A historical province in northwest Ethiopia, later also known as Gonder after its 20th-century capital.

amba-mariam.name: Maqdala
amba-mariam.summary: A village in central Ethiopia, known as Magdala or Maqdala during the reign of Emperor Tewodros II (1855–1868).

ethio-djibouti-railways.name: Ethio-Djibouti Railways
ethio-djibouti-railways.summary: A metre-gauge railway built between 1897 and 1917 linking Addis Ababa to Djibouti, giving landlocked Ethiopia its first access to the sea before falling into disrepair after World War II.

anno-mundi.name: Anno Mundi
anno-mundi.summary: A calendar era counting years from the biblical creation of the world, still used in the Hebrew calendar and formerly by Eastern Orthodox Christians until 1728.

pope-anianus-of-alexandria.name: Anianus
pope-anianus-of-alexandria.summary: Second Patriarch of Alexandria, ordained by Mark the Evangelist and said to be his first convert to Christianity in the region.

panodorus-of-alexandria.name: Panodoros era
panodorus-of-alexandria.summary: A world-era calendar system introduced by the Egyptian monk and historian Panodorus around 400 CE, counting years from the creation of the world to date events.

kingdom-of-kaffa.name: Kingdom of Kaffa
kingdom-of-kaffa.summary: A kingdom in the Ethiopian highlands from 1390 to 1897, homeland of the coffee plant and origin of its name, conquered and annexed by the Ethiopian Empire under Menelik II.

ankober.name: Ankober
ankober.summary: A town on the Ethiopian Highlands' escarpment, formerly capital of the kingdom of Shewa founded in the 13th century, from which Menelik moved his capital to Mount Entoto in 1884.

mount-entoto.name: Mount Entoto
mount-entoto.summary: Highest peak overlooking Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, where Emperor Menelik moved his capital in 1884 before founding the city nearby.

taytu-betul.name: Taytu Betul
taytu-betul.summary: Empress of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913 and third wife of Emperor Menelik II, an influential anti-colonial figure who co-founded Addis Ababa in 1886.

bank-of-abyssinia.name: Bank of Abyssinia
bank-of-abyssinia.summary: Ethiopia's first modern bank, established in 1905 and inaugurated by Emperor Menelik II in 1906; it produced the country's first banknotes in 1915.

national-bank-of-egypt.name: National Bank of Egypt
national-bank-of-egypt.summary: Egypt's largest bank, founded in 1898, historically influential enough to grant a concession that helped establish Ethiopia's Bank of Abyssinia in 1905.

metemma.name: Metemma
metemma.summary: A town in northwestern Ethiopia on the border with Sudan, facing the Sudanese village of Gallabat across the frontier.

sahle-selassie.name: Sahle Selassie
sahle-selassie.summary: King of Shewa in Ethiopia from 1813 to 1847, an important Amhara noble and great-grandfather of Haile Selassie, the last Emperor of Ethiopia.

negus.name: Negus
negus.summary: The Ethiopian Semitic word for king, traditionally granted to regional rulers by the Emperor, or 'King of Kings.'

sultanate-of-ifat.name: Sultanate of Ifat
sultanate-of-ifat.summary: Medieval Muslim state in the Horn of Africa, also called Wafāt or the Kingdom of Zeila, ruled by the Walashma dynasty between the late 13th and early 15th centuries.

tulama.name: Tulama Oromo
tulama.summary: An Oromo subgroup inhabiting the Shewa zones of Oromia in Ethiopia.

battle-of-gura.name: Battle of Gura
battle-of-gura.summary: The decisive second major battle of the Ethiopian-Egyptian War, fought 7-10 March 1876 near Gura in Eritrea, ending in Egyptian defeat.

beta-israel.name: Beta Israel
beta-israel.summary: Jewish community originating in the Amhara and Tigray regions of northern Ethiopia, historically practicing a distinct non-Talmudic form of Judaism; most have emigrated to Israel since 1979.

mahdist-war.name: Mahdist War
mahdist-war.summary: The 1881-1899 conflict between Sudanese Mahdist forces and, first, Egypt and then Britain, ending with the Anglo-Egyptian reconquest of Sudan and the fall of the Mahdist state.

falash-mura.name: Falash Mura
falash-mura.summary: Descendants of Ethiopia's Beta Israel community who converted to Christianity, mainly through Western missionary influence in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; many have since emigrated to Israel.

muhammad-ahmad.name: Muhammad Ahmad (the Mahdi)
muhammad-ahmad.summary: A Sudanese religious and political leader who declared himself the Mahdi in 1881, led a war against Egyptian rule, and founded an Islamic state that lasted until 1899.

samuel-gobat.name: Samuel Gobat
samuel-gobat.summary: Swiss-born Calvinist who became an Anglican missionary and Protestant Bishop of Jerusalem from 1846 until his death in 1879.

haymanot.name: Haymanot
haymanot.summary: The branch of Judaism practiced by the Beta Israel, or Ethiopian Jews; the word itself means "religion" or "faith" in Geʽez, Tigrinya and Amharic.

ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo-church.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
ethiopian-orthodox-tewahedo-church.summary: The largest Oriental Orthodox church, tracing back to the Christianization of Aksum in 330 CE, with tens of millions of adherents and one of only a few Oriental Orthodox churches in Africa.

ogaden.name: Ogaden
ogaden.summary: A plateau region in eastern Ethiopia inhabited mainly by Somalis, marked by over a century of self-determination movements following Ethiopian annexation in the 1890s.

ali-i-of-yejju.name: Ali I of Yejju
ali-i-of-yejju.summary: Ras of Begemder and regent of the Ethiopian Emperor who died in 1788, said to have founded the town of Debre Tabor, which became his dynasty's capital.

poulaine.name: Poulaines
poulaine.summary: A style of unisex footwear with extremely long, pointed toes, fashionable in medieval Europe from the mid-14th century and linked to bunions and falls; some rulers taxed or banned them.

wollo-province.name: Wollo
wollo-province.summary: A historical province of northern Ethiopia, known in the Middle Ages as Bete Amhara and the centre of the Solomonic dynasty founded around Lake Hayq in 1270.

dire-dawa.name: Dire Dawa
dire-dawa.summary: City in eastern Ethiopia, one of only two chartered cities in the country (with the capital Addis Ababa), and today an industrial centre with major markets.

jimma.name: Jimma
jimma.summary: The largest city in southwestern Oromia Region, Ethiopia, and its own special administrative zone.

waaq.name: Waaqism
waaq.summary: The pre-Muslim monotheistic faith of Cushitic peoples of the Horn of Africa, centered on Waaq, the sky god, whose name still means 'God' in Oromo.

pope-gregory-xvi.name: Pope Gregory XVI
pope-gregory-xvi.summary: Head of the Catholic Church and leader of the Papal States from 1831 to 1846, a staunch defender of traditional doctrine who condemned the slave trade in an 1839 papal brief.

wube-haile-maryam.name: Wube Haile Maryam
wube-haile-maryam.summary: 19th-century Ethiopian regional ruler (1799-1867) of Semien who conquered Tigray, was known for harsh military raids, and was defeated and imprisoned in 1855 by the future emperor Tewodros II.

congregation-of-the-mission.name: Lazarists
congregation-of-the-mission.summary: Common name for the Congregation of the Mission, a Catholic society of priests founded by Vincent de Paul.
